title: The Strange Situation
text:
Mary Ainsworth had watched mothers and babies at home, first in Uganda and then in Baltimore, taking careful notes on how mothers responded to crying, feeding and play. To compare children more systematically, she and her colleagues designed a short laboratory procedure for one-year-olds that became known as the Strange Situation.

A mother and her baby entered a playroom full of toys. A friendly stranger came in. Then the mother left for a few minutes, came back, left again, and returned once more. The researchers paid special attention not to how much the baby cried when she left, but to what happened when she came back.

Most babies, whom Ainsworth called securely attached, protested or missed their mother, greeted her warmly on her return, were soothed quickly and went back to play. Others seemed indifferent and avoided her when she returned. A third group was clingy and angry at once, seeking the mother yet resisting comfort. Later researchers added a fourth, disorganized pattern.

The home observations mattered most. Mothers who had responded sensitively and promptly to their babies' signals during the first year tended to have securely attached children. The babies had learned, from hundreds of small moments, whether care could be counted on.
lesson: A child's confidence is built from many ordinary moments in which you notice and respond. How you return after an absence matters as much as how you leave.
people: Mary Ainsworth, Mary Blehar, Everett Waters, Sally Wall
source: Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., and Wall, S. (1978). Patterns of Attachment: A Psychological Study of the Strange Situation. Hillsdale, NJ: Erlbaum.
